content: The term WASH in health care facilities refers to the provision of essential services and infrastructure for water, sanitation, hygiene, health care waste management, and environmental cleaning across all areas of a health care facility. These facilities may be located in either urban or rural settings. WASH services are critical for delivering quality health care. Without these services, achieving health goals—such as reducing maternal and neonatal mortality, curbing the spread of antimicrobial resistance, and preventing and containing disease outbreaks—becomes unattainable. Furthermore, WASH services significantly impact the experience of care. For example, functional and accessible toilets with menstrual hygiene facilities and safe drinking water uphold the dignity of patients and staff while fulfilling basic human rights. With renewed global focus on primary health care through the Astana Declaration and efforts to prevent early childhood deaths via the Every Child Alive Campaign, addressing WASH in health systems has become more urgent than ever. The 2019 baseline report from the WHO and UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) highlights the inadequacy of WASH services in health care facilities worldwide. Approximately 2 billion people lack access to basic water services, and 1.5 billion lack sanitation services in health care facilities. Many more are served by facilities without hand hygiene materials or proper waste segregation. WASH services are more commonly available in hospitals and urban areas compared to non-hospital facilities and rural settings. Non-hospital facilities are twice as likely to lack water or sanitation services, and urban areas generally have better WASH services than rural areas. Significant data gaps exist, particularly regarding hand hygiene, health care waste management, and cleaning practices. WHO and UNICEF have collected data from 125 countries, covering over 560,000 health care facilities. The JMP updates global figures every two years, with the next report planned for 2021. Efforts are underway to integrate global WASH indicators into national monitoring systems and external surveys. Advocacy for such inclusion is essential to improve data availability, enabling smarter actions and greater accountability. Since the launch of the global action plan on WASH in health care facilities in 2015, standards for WASH have been incorporated into many global health tools and are actively implemented in over 40 countries with government leadership and support from 35 partners. In 2018, the WHO/UNICEF JMP developed a harmonized set of global WASH indicators for health care facilities, which are now used to report progress on Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6. These indicators have been integrated into national health information systems, health facility assessments, and specific programs focusing on maternal and child health, vaccines, cholera, sepsis, and neglected tropical diseases. The WHO/UNICEF WASH Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT), which uses a quality improvement approach to address WASH risks, has been implemented in over 20 countries. In March 2018, the UN Secretary-General issued a global call to action on WASH in health care facilities, urging committed leadership and accountability for providing WASH services in all health care settings. The global call to action has led to the establishment of global targets for achieving universal access to WASH in health care facilities. These targets include ensuring that 60% of all health care facilities globally and in each SDG region have at least basic WASH services by 2022, 80% by 2025, and 100% by 2030. For countries that have already achieved universal basic WASH services, higher service levels are to be defined and monitored by 2022, with universal achievement of these higher levels by 2030 in 80% of such countries. To make progress, countries can take eight practical steps: conduct a situational analysis and assessment; set targets and define a national roadmap; establish national standards and accountability mechanisms; improve and maintain infrastructure; monitor progress and review data; develop the health workforce; engage communities; and conduct operational research and share learning. These steps are further detailed in the Practical Steps to Achieve Universal Access document, which includes country examples. Implementation of these steps will vary based on national priorities and contexts. Member States, UN agencies, and partners are encouraged to commit to action. Over 35 partners and UN agencies have already made concrete commitments to improve WASH in health care facilities. The next step is to secure universal, action-focused commitments on WASH at international, regional, national, and local levels. Mechanisms to support and track progress include a draft World Health Assembly resolution on WASH in health care facilities, which was sponsored by 10 Member States and unanimously approved by the WHO Executive Board in January 2019. This resolution calls for Member States to engage in the eight practical steps, starting with national assessments, roadmaps, and new targets and standards for WASH in health care facilities. Member States will report progress to WHO every two years. Additionally, data on coverage compiled by the WHO/UNICEF JMP and data on policies and targets compiled by the UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water are key mechanisms for assessing progress. Countries across all regions are taking action on some or all of the eight practical steps. Examples include Cambodia conducting a health systems situational analysis, Ghana developing a national costed WASH strategy for health care facilities, Serbia and Lebanon creating national standards, Tanzania strengthening the cleaning workforce, Liberia providing mentoring and supervision to improve services, and Indonesia, the Philippines, Nepal, and Vietnam adopting green health care waste management approaches. These efforts demonstrate that significant progress can be made even in resource-limited settings. The public can support the UN Secretary-General’s Call to Action by understanding the WASH situation in their country. If data are unavailable, communities and health care facility users should demand that health authorities and facility managers track and share data on WASH services. Care seekers should recognize that access to safe water and sanitation is a fundamental right and should participate in designing and improving WASH services. They should also advocate for clean, safe health care facilities with accessible toilets and safe drinking water. Additionally, health care providers should be held accountable for practicing good hand hygiene and serving as role models for the community. For more information, the WHO/UNICEF WASH in health care facilities website provides tools, technical guidance, country case studies, news, and updates. You can also sign up for regular updates through the WHO/UNICEF WASH newsletter.
